lesson.title: How Pure Is Pure: Determining Percent Purity by Titration
lesson.summary: Percent purity uses a titration's stoichiometry to determine what fraction of an impure sample's mass is actually the reactive substance of interest.
lesson.body:
Percent purity asks what fraction of a sample, by mass, is actually the substance of interest, with the rest being inert impurities that do not react during the titration. It is a close cousin of percent yield: percent yield compares an actual amount produced to a theoretical amount predicted by stoichiometry, while percent purity compares an actual amount of active substance present in an already obtained sample to the sample's total measured mass. Both are, at their core, a ratio of an experimentally determined amount to a reference amount, expressed as a percentage.

Titration calculations are a natural way to measure percent purity when the substance of interest reacts in a known, clean stoichiometric way, because the same four step procedure already gives you the moles, and therefore the mass, of the pure active substance actually present, regardless of what else is mixed in with it. Anything inert in the sample simply does not react with the titrant and does not affect the result, as long as it does not interfere with the indicator or the reaction itself.

Suppose a 1.500 g sample of solid sodium hydroxide, known to contain some non-reactive impurities picked up from storage, is dissolved in water and titrated with 0.2000 M HCl, requiring 165.0 mL to reach the equivalence point. The reaction is one to one: NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l). Moles of HCl delivered: 0.1650 L x 0.2000 mol/L = 0.03300 mol, which equals moles of NaOH actually present in the sample, since the ratio is 1:1.

Converting moles of pure NaOH to mass using its molar mass, 40.00 g/mol: 0.03300 mol x 40.00 g/mol = 1.320 g. That 1.320 g is the mass of genuine NaOH in the sample, out of the 1.500 g total sample mass that was weighed out. Percent purity is that ratio times 100: 1.320 g / 1.500 g x 100 = 88.0 percent. The remaining 12.0 percent of the sample's mass, 0.180 g, is whatever inert material, likely absorbed water or carbonate, was mixed in with the NaOH.

Percent purity calculated this way is only as reliable as the assumption that nothing else in the sample reacts with the titrant. If an impurity happened to also be acidic or basic, it would react too, be counted as if it were the substance of interest, and inflate the calculated purity, which is exactly why a real analysis usually pairs a titration purity result with an independent qualitative check on what the impurities actually are.
